speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion concerning an urgent and important matter.
Last March 7, along with 17 government members, I visited the authorities of the port of Montreal. We saw then that a serious problem threatened the economic future of that port and might cause the loss of hundreds of jobs not only in the constituency of Hochelaga, but also in the neighbouring constituencies. Given the answer made last Thursday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Dupont), to the effect that it was not appropriate to make any comments at this stage, and considering that several thousands of related workers in the port of Montreal as well as 1,200 longshoremen are involved, and that the company appears to have decided to leave the port of Montreal, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle):

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-AGREEMENT WITH BOEING AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I believe affects the rights of all members of this House. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) does well to put down his documents, because this also affects him.
My question of privilege arises out of an agreement between the Minister of Justice of Canada and his counterpart in the United States. It has already been the subject of exchanges

March 16, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Baldwin
between myself and the minister. The right of members of this House to inquire about the expenditure of public funds is as old and as cherished as the institution itself. Our rights today are so limited that any attempt sensibly to diminish them further must be regarded with alarm and form the subject of such a question of privilege as I am now raising. I shall be very brief because the issue is plain.
The agreement in question provides that with respect to information gathered covering the potential illegal sales arrangements or considerations or activities of Boeing aircraft and all its subsidiaries in Canada there is an understanding reached between the ministers, between the two attorneys general, which covers this particular activity of the Boeing company. Part IV provides that except as provided in paragraph 5, which deals with taking criminal and other legal proceedings, all such information made available by the parties pursuant to these procedures, that is, the procedures for gathering information, and all correspondence between the parties relating to such information and to the implementation of these procedures shall be kept confidential by both parties and shall not be disclosed to third parties, including government agencies having no law enforcement responsibilities- which, of course, covers this parliament, the House of Commons and all its members.
This agreement is a solemn convenant between two high officials of two governments to operate as a gag rule to prevent knowledge of certain facts being brought to the attention of members of parliament. It is not enough just to have criminal proceedings taken. The Minister of Justice may have in his possession a large number of documents and a great deal of material and information. All he has to do is make a conscious decision not to go ahead with criminal proceedings or, if he does, to limit the information to very specific cases. Everything else can go into the shredder, and there is no way under those conditions in which members of this House can discharge their constitutional responsibility to make an inquiry as to what are the facts.

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-AGREEMENT WITH BOEING AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-AGREEMENT WITH BOEING AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
As my hon. friend from Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) has said, if the Public Accounts Committee or the Auditor General in the discharge of their parliamentary duties saw fit to call before them government officials, they would be prevented by the terms of this agreement from gathering the facts which would be essential to making a parliamentary inquiry. I am not talking about criminal proceedings. That is outside our jurisdiction at this moment. But there are collateral inquiries governing issues of potential impropriety and misdemeanours which from time to time need to be the subject of an inquiry under the Inquiries Act, by this House or by a committee of parliament.
For these reasons, I say the agreement to which I have referred is an invidious and improper one, curtailing as it does the rights of members of this House, and if Your Honour holds that there is a prima facie case of privilege I would move,

seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr.-Baker):
That this House demand that the government explain fully the circumstances leading to this imprudent and dangerous agreement and, furthermore, on the basis that parliament has the primary responsibility to inquire into the proper expenditure of the taxpayers' money for the purchase of aircraft and supplies from Boeing Aircraft, that the agreement of March 15 and related circumstances be referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

subsubtopic: MR. BALDWIN-AGREEMENT WITH BOEING AIRCRAFT

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief. I do not have a copy of the agreement in front of me, so I am unable to cite chapter and verse. But there is no question of privilege involved here, and to suggest otherwise is specious. It is clear from the terms of the agreement that it is drawn up in accordance with the domestic laws of the requesting and the requested states. Mr. Speaker, I am joined in the motion and I want to say I question strongly the position which has been taken so blandly by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) that the right of parliament to know about matters which may be under investigation and in respect of which criminal charges have not been laid, and therefore our right to discuss and question these matters, has not been infringed.
The Minister of Justice said he felt the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) was advancing a specious argument. I must say, if it is the position of the Minister of Justice that information will be denied parliament, and that is what the agreement says, that information will be denied to members of parliament or to the public accounts committee, that certain information will be denied to the servant of parliament, the Auditor General, I cannot see how, with respect to any matter that is being investigated and with respect to which a charge has not been laid, the minister can stand up and hide behind an agreement made outside this place. If ever there was a specious argument, it is the one advanced by the minister.
One more thing, Mr. Speaker. With regard to the level of secrecy involved, which may be normal, the first paragraph of the agreement recites that all requests for assistance shall be communicated between the parties through diplomatic channels. I can just hear how the minister of external affairs, the parliamentary facsimile of Ivan Head, would deal with the matter if someone ever had the temerity to ask a question. What this agreement does is effectively bypass parliament's right to question, parliament's right to information, and the servant of parliament's right to information. I do not suspect that the Minister of Justice has taken leave of his senses, but I do think that his observations with respect to what is right and what is wrong, in terms of disclosure to parliament, indicate that his attitude to parliament is all wrong. Surely this place, as much as the Minister of Justice, has the right to know.
March 16, 1977

This agreement with the Boeing company, its subsidiaries or affiliates, does not strangle parliament, but it does close a door on parliament. In that sense my rights and the rights of all members to question are affected and I hope Your Honour will so find.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, March 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-24, respecting immigration to Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night before the adjournment of the debate I was canvassing the situation with regard to the present Immigration Act. I had a number of very serious criticisms to make with regard to the application of the act, the introduction of regulations and the postulate that these regulations have expressed the will of parliament, and a number of other points. I do not retract any of the statements I made last night.
Now I should like to turn to the bill before us. I want to make it very clear that while I have some pertinent questions to raise with regard to some of the clauses as they now appear, I think the present legislation, in some respects, is an improvement on the previous act and its application, and therefore it should receive the approval of the House to at least send it to committee where representations will be made. I have heard

the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) and others on the government side say that representations will be made on behalf of various interested persons and that the minister and his officials will be questioned much more closely as to the intent in the administration of the act and its interpretation, and also that the minister and his officials will have an opportunity to introduce the regulations. That point should be almost non-negotiable for the further passage of this legislation beyond the report stage. The regulations should be there to be seen, because they are the heart and core of this act. I hope the House will agree, either later this day or at a very early opportunity, with the sending of this bill to the committee for further consideration. It is not acceptance in principle.
There are a number of points that I want to raise with regard to the bill. Under clause 12 it is proposed, quite rightly so, that every applicant for landed immigrant status in Canada shall appear before an immigration officer. That is understandable. But what concerns me is that now, in many ports of entry, the immigration officer in the first line is a customs officer. It is not every Tom, Dick and Harry who is trained and qualified to be a customs officer who should be an immigration officer. An immigration officer is a man of particular skill who has important decisions to make. True enough, if the first-line immigration officer has any question about the application of the applicant, then it passes on to a second-line examination carried out, I understand, by an immigration officer, not a customs officer.
I have a particular interest in the Department of National Revenue, and 1 know the problems they are having with the customs officers. I understand that adequate steps will be taken-and this is a point I will make on another occasion-to provide adequate facilities for the better training of our customs officers so they can cope with both customs problems and immigration problems. It may be a training college or some other facility, but it would be more than just passing an examination of the public service. The requirement would be attendance at a familiarization course of indeterminate duration and then being placed at a port of entry where that individual would perform both as a customs and an immigration officer. If this first-line immigration officer is merely a reader of stamps and visas to see whether the page conforms with what has been laid down in some manual, then I question the value of that requirement. But if that person is going to be a functioning immigration officer, then let us be sure that he is adequately trained and has the adequate background knowledge of the Immigration Act and the regulations, that his decision shall be reviewable and that there shall be a second-line decision. This is one point to which I take grave exception.
Applicants for immigration to Canada, under the present act, who are in the field arrive at a decision with regard to the assessment of points or other factors. If the total does not add up, the decision is not reviewable. That is totally wrong. It is an injustice to the individual concerned or any individual representing that person. As a man who has had a great deal to do with immigration, I do not want to see this practice continue under the act. There must be a procedure developed
March 16, 1977

within the department. It is not a question of going to the Immigration Appeal Board, but there again I am uncertain because I have also serious doubts as to civil rights and natural justice in the denial of access to the Immigration Appeal Board. Frankly, between what was passed two or three years ago with the limitation on the Immigration Appeal Board Act and the changes embodied in this act, I could almost say that the Immigration Appeal Board is a superfluous luxury.
The jurisdiction and the administration of that board which have been introduced into the immigration process on account of rights and justice have been cut away, frittered, although not entirely, but I think also the board has become too much like a court. Members of the board have imposed upon themselves certain rules which I think were not intended. So I think the whole question of the Immigration Appeal Board should be reviewed. It is not exactly relevant to discuss it here, but I have the report of the Law Reform Commission of Canada with regard to the Immigration Appeal Board.
I suggest that the report of the Law Reform Commission of Canada with regard to the Immigration Appeal Board be referred to a House committee for examination, because it makes some strong recommendations with regard to the workings of that board. I think that there should be some changes to the Immigration Appeal Board Act, but not those brought forward by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), who himself is subject to the jurisdiction of the Immigration Appeal Board. In other words, the minister makes himself the prosecutor and the judge by bringing forward legislation which controls the Immigration Appeal Board, to which he later must submit. .How do we load the dice? There will have to be some answers to that question.
There is another point to which I would like to refer. As I recall it, this bill says that there shall be no discrimination on the grounds of race, creed, colour-practically everything except age. For years I have been fighting the Department of Manpower and Immigration over its points system and with regard to penalties against people over age 35. I have been saying that this has been a practical denial of the government's stated intention that there should be no discrimination as to age. The public is not supposed to discriminate against people with regard to employment or any other thing on the ground of age, but the regulations under the Immigration Act say that that is allowable. I say that is wrong. I suggest that Bill C-24 is in contravention of clause 8 of Bill C-25. Clause 8 of Bill C-25 reads as follows:
It is a discriminatory practice
(a)	to use or circulate any form of application for employment, or
(b)	in connection with employment or prospective employment,
(i)	to publish any advertisement, or
(ii)	to make any written or oral inquiry that expresses or implies any limitation, specification or preference based on a prohibited ground of discrimination.
Discrimination on the ground of age is prohibited, and under the Immigration Act as it is presently applied-under Manpower form 1234-in any inquiry with regard to employment
Immigration Act
there can be an inquiry as to age. That is now to be prohibited under Bill C-25 but not under Bill C-24. Since this immigration legislation is to be geared to manpower requirements- and that is the prime purpose of Bill C-24-an inquiry as to the age of a prospective immigrant and the allocation of points based upon age is, I suggest, in flagrant contravention of clause 8 of Bill C-25. 1 am glad to see, for instance, that with respect to reunification of families, parents under the age of 60 will be admitted regardless of Manpower form 1234. That is a big step forward, because there has been great heartbreak and difficulty because parents aged 45, 50 or 55 have been "totally unemployable" in this country.
These people have been considered to be totally unemployable in areas where the officials have said there should not be any admission of unskilled labour. They are talking about the service industries where people can act as assistant managers in local restaurants. To the officials, that is an unskilled occupation. They think that working in a kitchen as an assistant cook is an unskilled occupation; but these immigrants know the language required, they have the necessary family connections and, 1 suppose, the ability to make a particular operation work. However, do not try to explain that to a bureaucrat. When you try to explain that to departmental officials, you get the blanket assertion, signed by the minister or any number of officials, that it is the policy not to admit any unskilled labour.
Who says they are unskilled? Is it Manpower? Do these people have to fall under the headings of bricklayer, carpenter, electrician, certified by a union or certified by a provincial labour board? I would like to see those who make that assertion try to operate those establishments and find out whether they are skilled or unskilled. Some of them could not operate a corner peanut stand, yet they call others unskilled. There has to be a complete change of thinking in this area.
Let me assure this House that all of Canada is not to be painted with the same bland brush. There are high demands today in certain areas of the country for so called unskilled labour. There is a crying need for people in some regions, and yet suitable prospective immigrants are turned down. We are told we can put Greeks into Chinese restaurants, or Italians into Hindu restaurants. This is the same throughout the service industries. I am told this in letter after letter. This nonsense is compounded by Manpower officials in the Department of Manpower and Immigration and sometimes by the human rights legislation of some provinces. This is just not practical.
I am hopeful that under clause 19 one of the carryovers of the old act will be eliminated. I refer to epileptics. The wording is not as clear as I would like it to be, because to me there are some weasel words of discretion which will make it very difficult in appropriate cases to get at the reason a medical officer who has different views from others will be more restrictive. I suppose I am getting back to the question whether the prospective immigrant or his or her representative can gain access to the information they need. In the past I have had experiences where people have been ruled not admis-
4042

March 16, 1977
Immigration Act
sible on medical grounds because of active tuberculosis. All that was required was a set of X-ray films examined by a radiologist and confirmed by a non-departmental official to determine that the original diagnosis was wrong. Over the years I have had many cases on simply that point. It is a question of being able to get at that information and question it. That is what I ask.
I raise another point which will have to come out in committee. The Immigration Appeal Board Act, which I do not have before me, provides that any person had a right to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board if the appeal is made within Canada. Somewhere along the line an innocuous-looking order in council was passed which said that "any person'' shall be defined as a "Canadian citizen." Therefore, we have the case of a landed immigrant, say a woman who has been here four years, marrying a person and not knowing that that person was not admissible to Canada. Perhaps he was here illegally. There could be extenuating circumstances which, for a number of reasons, one could argue before the Immigration Appeal Board. But, Mr. Speaker, unless that wife is a Canadian citizen there are no grounds for appeal and deportation must follow, even though the spouse in this country could then apply to bring the other spouse in from the other country, subject to ministerial approval. Mr. Speaker, how cruel; how wrong! What right is there, when the statute speaks of "any person", to abuse the right to pass regulations by saying that "any person" shall be limited to "Canadian citizen"?
To me, that is one of the orders in council that before the statutory instruments committee should be struck down because it is an abuse. That order in council, limiting the definition in that way, is entirely contrary to the spirit of the statute. But it made things very much simpler for the Department of Immigration. It applied a restriction on the Immigration Appeal Board, or the rights of persons to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board which might rule against the decisions of immigration officers. That order in council, to me, is a denial of justice and a denial-indeed, an abuse-of the parliamentary process.
I hope that in the regulations we shall see some clarification of that much abused term "moral turpitude" which has been used, like some of the general orders, in the Queen's regulations. If you cannot find anything else with which to charge a person, you allege that he or she was guilty of moral turpitude. Even the signing of a statutory declaration, which the person did not understand, signing under pressure from the spouse, was deemed to be moral turpitude and an excuse to exclude the wife of a man already in Canada as a landed immigrant. I hope that we shall get some explanation of section 10, and that students will not be limited to university and other institutions over and above high school. There are so many young people who must clear up one or two subjects.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you and hon. members of the House. I shall take only three or four minutes to make some positive suggestions which I want to see included in the regulations and in the statute. I think we have accomplished a great deal in our program of immigration by admitting students who have come into this country to finish their high school education so they can be eligible for university entrance. The trouble is that the requirements for university entrance are not uniform across Canada. Why say, then, that they shall all be qualified for university entrance only? Why cannot we bring them in, perhaps to improve their English? There are institutions, colleges and high schools which would do this. I have no difficulty introducing high school students to high schools in Edmonton on a selective basis. The classes are half empty in some places, and they are happy to do it. I am thinking of Mount Royal College, Calgary, and Concordia College in Edmonton, which can prepare students for university according to the standards of the university they have chosen. But section 10, unless amended by regulation, prohibits that. I think that is wrong. There should be more flexibility in that section.
Also, I want to see something done about the regulations and the application of those regulations with regard to special inquiries. I have read transcripts of special inquiries which to me, as a lawyer, cry out as an abuse of justice. They were filled with hearsay evidence, unexplained requirements, and so on. Individuals were intimidated by the very nature of the formal process. Frankly, they did not have a nickel's chance of beating the rap, to use that term, unless accompanied by counsel well versed in what goes on at special inquiries. Over the years I have read transcripts of some special inquiries and if those proceedings had been taken against the criminal it would have taken a court of appeal less than ten seconds to throw them out.
Also, why should the criminal have a higher right than the poor individual coming in as an immigrant? This process must be looked at, Mr. Speaker. If a special inquiry officer makes a decision, that should be reviewable on the spot by a senior officer, not somebody far removed, as now, at regional headquarters or headquarters. Why do I say this? A special inquiry officer may order the detention of a person, just like that, and it is not appealable. I also say this-and let me say here that I exchanged correspondence with the minister and I know the problems he is facing-that in Edmonton if detention is ordered by a special inquiry officer, it will be at the Fort Saskatchewan jail.
Mr. Speaker, there can be no more inhuman decision taken than that taken by special inquiry officers to place men or women into that common tank, that jail of hardened criminals. There is no requirement at the present time for separate facilities which would have to be maintained full-time. I would invite the minister, the deputy minister or anybody else to
March 16, 1977

accompany me into the tank at Fort Saskatchewan jail and see the conditions to which they submit persons who have not been guilty of a criminal act but for some reason or another have run afoul of the Immigration Act. They would not force that upon the meanest cur, but they would do it to a fellow human being. I protest that. Hopefully, negotiations are under way with the appropriate provincial authorities so that there will be adequate detention facilities for persons charged under the Immigration Act-but not the criminal tank. That is not their place.
I have had a lot to say about this act. I hope my colleagues in this House will allow me to appear at the committee when we have hearings because I am firmly dedicated to getting a most workable and humane Immigration Act. I have had 20 years' experience as a member of parliament and have fought many cases before the Immigration Appeal Board. Incidentally, I have not lost one of those I have taken to the Immigration Appeal Board. I can assure the minister that when it comes to the interpretation of the law in so far as those two acts are concerned, his officials have not been quite up to the mark in those cases where I have appeared. At least, the board has always ruled in favour of some poor individual.
We have to get a workable Immigration Act that responds to the needs of the country and the people. They shall not be mere chattels or cattle that we will be importing. We shall not handle them in this country any different than we handle Canadian citizens. They are human beings and they have the dignity of human beings. To direct an immigrant to go to such and such a place under penalty, or possible penalty of expulsion if that person should move, is not right. We would not do it to one of our fellow citizens. We have a great job to do with this act. I hope that parliament, in its wisdom, will accomplish it. I hope I have the opportunity of contributing in that respect.
I commend to my colleagues the passage of this bill to go to the committee so that we can introduce the necessary amendments and have the necessary explanations. Since many of us who could not attend the public hearings have a great deal of experience on all facets of immigration, perhaps we could make a contribution. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the House for these additional moments.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill under study contains statements of principle which, at first glance, invite our support. However, for a country like ours immigration is becoming a vital question, considering that through immigration we can or could control in a way the very nature of our country. Otherwise we would be ignoring the fact that different nations exist in this country. And since November 15, that fact has no doubt become more obvious.
Indeed, we saw last week the Quebec minister of immigration object to at least some provisions of this bill. I would like, Mr. Speaker, to deal with some of the factors which make immigration a sensitive question in Canada. Of course, we
Immigration Act
ought not to fall into generalizations and charges such as those the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) indulged in last night when she said that the Quebec minister of immigration was being racist in his statements on immigration.
Mr. Speaker, that is absolutely not the question. We all know that every man should at the outset be considered as perfectly equal, no matter his colour, race, religion; this is obvious and of course I agree with that as does every one else in the House. But one would be blind not to find that to this day immigration in Canada has been a self-destructing factor for the province of Quebec, since immigration in Quebec has always been contrary to the national interests of French Canadians of Quebec. I would much rather it were not so, Mr. Speaker. But the strongest evidence of that lies in famous Bill 22. For some years now, the successive Quebec governments have all tried to deal with the language problem in Quebec, and up till now they have all failed and all met with disastrous consequences.
Mr. Speaker, Bill 22 would never have been introduced if immigration in Quebec had been dealt with normally but, as it was always dealt with abnormally, it follows that when the people demand that things be set straight which were always upside down, some think that they are revolutionaries who want to destroy everything. But, Mr. Speaker, nothing is to be destroyed at all when one says that it would be normal for anyone, regardless of where he comes from in the world, who decides to come and live in Quebec, for that person to integrate into the spirit of the majority of the people in Quebec. Is there anything more normal than that?
But for years and years the opposite happened, with the result that in the province of Quebec, where only about 4 per cent of the population are of Anglo-Saxon origin-yes, only 4 per cent in the whole of Quebec-16 per cent are still Anglophones in a Francophone province. Why? Because immigrants continually joined the minority instead of the majority, so much so that they had better schools than the majority.
They had more English-speaking universities in Quebec than there were French-speaking universities. The minority had more universities than the majority. And yet we Quebec taxpayers paid more from our own pocket to allow such a situation. This is ridiculous, as much as all Canada is ridiculous, and this is why we will have to reconsider the whole thing some day. In the meantime, when the minister introduces legislation concerning such a vital matter as immigration, it is very important to establish priorities. One of them already exists, and the minister admits it, for his bill refers to consultations with the provinces. It would have been shocking to leave out this priority.
But I think this legislation is deficient because it provides for consultations but not for a government priority as regards immigration. Although the Canadian constitution allows both the federal government and the provinces to deal with immigration, we should be wise enough in this parliament to decide

that the priority should go to the provinces. In my opinion, there is nothing to argue about it.
Obviously the problem is not as acute in the provinces with an overwhelming English-speaking majority. Of course I understand that this matter is of secondary importance for most Canadian provinces but its essential and vital importance to Quebec should be recognized. Therefore I can only agree when the minister responsible for immigration in Quebec says categorically and clearly that an agreement is required in this area.
I understand that we could trust the honesty of the federal government but, Mr. Speaker, the people of Quebec know what that means. We have trusted it for years and where are we now? The effect has been that more often than not we are second-class citizens, who are full of complexes and who ask themselves to what extent they can consider Canada as their own country. This is where we are now. Therefore others seem to be aware of this now. It is strange that this awareness comes at a time when Quebec is on the verge of independence and that we have been waiting so long, but these are the facts.
So I think that the government should display a more efficient flexibility and when it legislates on matters such as immigration it should at least realize that in that field the province of Quebec must have priority. That is why I feel consultations are not sufficient. Mr. Speaker, everybody knows that we almost have dictatorship with the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). We know very well that consultations can sometimes amount to precious little and if we go back to November 14, 1976, we all recall that the Prime Minister was still taking the liberty of saying to the provinces: whether or not you accept it, that is what is going to be done. So he said.
He did it again. Even in the evening of November 15, his first reaction was not a wise one but rather he said: we are going to organize Levesque and his government. His first reaction was one of disillusion, like somebody who wants to kick over the traces. Mr. Speaker, since that time he has become almost bland and he wants to change everything. He is ready to do anything. We do not know what, however, but he said he would go as far as amending the constitution. If he is ready to do all that, he should begin by making changes in his bills so as to prove his good will, because people have had enough talk. Quebec has had enough. We want action, we want proof that federalism is worthwhile, that it will not continue to be a burden for us. So, to prove it, things must be made clear when such a bill is introduced. That is what I find unfortunate, and I think that it is so important that failing to think of solving that problem would prove there is no intent on his part to solve all other problems.
But that problem, Mr. Speaker, is so important, so essential that I wonder if, before introducing his bill, the minister should not have met the authorities of other provinces, especially the province of Quebec. Then he could have introduced the bill and said that he had the agreement of all provincial ministers responsible; we would have been able then to discuss the subject matter, its form, and reach a worthwhile and efficient conclusion.

But since that was not done, we are faced once more with a dilemma. I gave a concrete example of this a minute ago while discussing Bill 22. Some members seemed surprised at my making a connection over this but, Mr. Speaker, I could come back to it for a few seconds to show that it is a fact. Who created problems with regards to Bill 22? It is common knowledge that it was the Italian community of Montreal. It was not the Anglo-Saxons since there are none in Quebec. The vast majority of English-speaking Quebecers are of Italian origin, plus many other nationalities; they did it. I understand them and do not blame them.
But the successive administrations in Quebec have always tolerated these abnormalities, that is why it seems revolutionary to talk of correcting them, as I said earlier. Nevertheless, truth always prevails and we must see things in their true perspective. And if there is a problem in Quebec today and that terrible mess about Bill 22, it is because we have not been diligent enough to give the responsibility with regards to immigration to those who are best able to judge in this respect and, this being so, the provincial authorities should have had such a responsibility. That is why I still hope that the consultations indicated in the bill will have some effect and bring about an understanding to define precisely the powers of the various levels of government in this area.
But fundamentally, I believe that these things had to be said in the House. We will have to consider more and more the possibility of amending this bill to establish clearly certain priorities for the control of immigration at the level of the Quebec administration. Once we have control over immigration at that level, we will have nothing else to criticize, to find fault with in the federal administration in this area. Indeed there are those who will jump to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, when considering the facts I have enumerated a while ago, that we are trying to drown systematically the French-speaking element in Quebec. I am not saying they are right, but considering the way things are going on, we are inclined to think so. This is why I think the minister has very well pointed out the advantages of this bill, putting particular emphasis on the consulting process with the provinces. He took pride in the fact that he had introduced this provision in the bill. I can only congratulate him for having done this. But, Mr. Speaker, consultation is not enough nowadays, in 1977. Terms of agreement have to be determined and this is nothing less than giving control over immigration to those who are able to give it a direction likely to favour emancipation and openness.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take too much of the time of the House, but there are some specific aspects of the bill with which I want to deal since I think that the ramifications of particular provisions for Canada's international relations are very serious indeed. Why I relate specific provisions to Canada's international relations is because of the Helsinki accord and our capacity as a nation to persuade countries that refuse to allow their citizens to leave,
March 16, 1977

such as the Soviet Union, Czechoslovakia and a good many of the eastern European countries, to observe that accord. If we are going to be successful in terms of persuading such countries that their citizens have the right of freedom of movement from one country to another, then why, in God's name, have we included in this bill clause 115( 1 )(n)? Let me read this provision, since I fear the significance of it has been lost to some extent on the general public and it should be brought to their attention:
The governor in council may make regulations ...
(n) requiring any person or class of persons to report to an immigration officer before leaving Canada and prescribing the information to be provided and the manner in which such report shall be made to the immigration officer by any such person-
Any plain reading of that provision leads me to the conclusion that this is the beginning of exit visas for Canadians. I am glad to see the minister is flipping through the bill, because I should like to hear his response. Surely it is hypocritical of this government to condemn the Soviet Union, Czechoslovakia, Poland and all the other countries who wrongfully refuse to allow their citizens to rejoin their families and who have violated the Helsinki accord, when the government inserts into this law the capacity to require exit visas for its own citizens before they leave this country.
The minister will probably say that this is a catch-all section, that the government is trying to catch some of the bad boys. Or he may say that this does not really apply to any particular person but refers only to illegal immigrants who are leaving the country. But the clause does not say that, Mr. Speaker. I have read what it says and I do not accept explanatory notes.
Clearly, there is authority under this provision to require exit visas for Canadians before they leave the country. If we are going to embark upon that route, I will feel awfully funny when I write to the local Czech charge d'affaires, as I have been doing to try to unify a family in my community, and as I am sure other members have who have similar cases, and ask why this oppressive regime does not allow the unification of families and why they continue to violate the Helsinki accord. The answer of the charge d'affaires at the Czechoslovakian embassy to me will be, "Look at clause 115(l)(n) of your own Immigration Act". He will say that all countries do this and we are no different from any other.
I urge the minister to withdraw this provision from the bill. The Helsinki accord cuts both ways, not just one way. We love to jump up and complain about other regimes, but let us look to home first and make sure that our act is clean. Then when the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) goes to the United Nations he will not have to hide clause 115(l)(n) when talking to his counterparts about their consistent violation of the Helsinki accord. I urge the government seriously to reconsider that particular provision. Although I have reservations about photographing and fingerprinting, to me this particular provision is the most iniquitous because it clearly gives the government power to restrict the movement of Canadian citizens from this country.
Immigration Act
I remember a long time ago we condemned the United States for refusing to allow a man called Paul Robeson to leave that country. The reason was that he was saying some very anti-American things abroad. He was complaining that society was racist and he was embarrassing his government. If a Canadian citizen wishes to leave this country and to criticize Canada, that is his right and I do not think we should restrict this kind of freedom of ideas under the provisions of this law.
I submit to the minister that what was done to Paul Robeson can clearly be done to any person in Canada no matter what are his political views. If this government did not want him to travel, they could clearly apply clause 115(1 )(n). This is one of the reasons out of many why we in this party will oppose this bill. We think this provision is so serious in terms of our international relations and the reunification of families in Canada that it strikes at the heart of the principle of what to some extent this country stands for, namely, the freedom to travel and to go abroad.
I am concerned, as many Canadians are, that we are dealing with the immigration bill at a time when we have officially one million people unemployed in Canada. At a time when we have high unemployment we face a very high risk in Canada of increasing racist tensions among people, particularly working people who feel far less secure about their employment and about the competition which may come from immigrant groups for their employment, and because of that increasing tension we have to be cautious about the approach we take to immigration. Some of the evidence that racism is growing in Canada need not be repeated. There are many examples of it. I am getting a little tired of going back to my riding and hearing someone in a men's club telling racist jokes. We should all look into ourselves and say that is not a respectable thing to do in this country; it is too dangerous.

I am tired of people who cloak racism under articles about immigration. The idea that we have to maintain a certain ethnic character in this country is an idea I reject. I think we can bring in people of whatever origin so long as they are needed in Canada. The problem up to now has been that we have not properly assessed our needs in terms of immigration. I do not see immigration as anybody's right to come to this country; I still say it is a privilege.
I know my friend, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), does not agree, but that is what makes our party so healthy. We have healthy disagreements on a number of questions. I say that those who see it as an excuse to apply racism in terms of their chance to deal with the unemployment situation should not be allowed to do so. I reject that out of hand. But we must consider immigration in terms of Canadian need.
The B.C. schools trustees association in my province recently made a decision that a film that had been made about the history of British Columbia which dealt with our own attitudes

to various racial groups, particularly the Chinese, the Japanese and the East Indian communities, should not be shown in those schools. The argument they used was that that kind of film would be inflammatory. I say that their refusal to allow the history of B.C. to be told in the school system is itself inflammatory, is itself wrong.
We have to expose the history of Canadians in terms of the racial tensions that have developed. I am including, of course, the problems with regard to the Japanese and the rotten record of the Liberal government of that time in dealing with the right of the native Japanese Canadians. We have a poor race record in Canada, and let us admit it. We have a bad record with regard to the toleration of other groups, and the sooner we get it out of the way, the faster we can move on to tolerating people of various ethnic backgrounds.
Let me say how this is related to this bill. I am delighted the bill clearly does not discriminate on the basis of national origin, and I must say that that is a feature in the bill which could almost persuade me to change my mind about voting against it on second reading, except for this fantastic power that is given in terms of the discretion under the regulations. That in itself is too bitter a pill to swallow, even in the face of what seems to be some improvement in other sections of the bill.
I want to deal now with another principle which this bill does not protect. There are visitors to this country and there are immigrants to this country. Once in a while we have a visitor to this country who has very radical ideas, ideas with which probably very few people would agree. I am referring to people whose ideas may be unpopular in this country. But we should not be afraid of ideas. Surely we should be able to explore ideas. I am referring to the recent case of Andre Frank and the refusal to allow him to come to this country. Mr. Frank had something to contribute to the academic life of this country, but he was denied access to Canada. We have done it before. We still seem to have trouble distinguishing between revolutionary ideas and people who might commit terrorist acts. I say that the record is a bad one in Canada. We err continually on the side of excluding those people with unpopular ideas who are no danger whatsoever to Canada. I think we are strong enough and big enough as a country to explore a whole range of ideas. A few of them might rub off, and this would not hurt us at all.
I do not want to take a long time on this bill. There are provisions in it which require fingerprinting and photographing. I should like to ask hon. members how they would feel if they were fingerprinted and photographed each time they entered another country. I realize that this again is under a regulation that can be narrowly interpreted. We would like to see it limited. We do not want to wait and hope that discretion will be exercised in a proper way, because there have been instances in the past when that discretion has not been exercised in a fair way.
I want to say that I stand this afternoon in opposition to the immigration bill. I accept the principle that we have to limit the population in Canada in accordance with our needs. I also

happen to think that this country does not need 50 million people.
I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is here. I remember his famous remark about that subject some years ago. I liked the population of Canada in 1939. It was a nice place at that time. We had a lot of room and our ecology was well protected. I do not think we need to have all this growthmanship of developing another giant on the north American continent. We can be cautious about population growth. We can set an example to the world in terms of the way we relate our environment and our geography to the number of people who are in Canada, and we can keep this country one of the most desirable countries in the world by having a reasonable program of family planning and a reasonable program-

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first reading of Bill C-24 took place on November 24 of last year. Since then I have been concerned about the approach of the government to this most important subject. When we brush aside the sweeping generalities and the gloss in the bill, the proposed legislation simply asks parliament to give the government and its advisers a free hand in establishing immigration programs of unknown and unspecified characteristics. This raises an important question: does this government's past performance justify the kind of trust it is now asking for?
I will not dwell on the weaknesses or the purpose contained in this badly written and questionable bill; spokesmen for our party have already covered this ground pretty thoroughly. But I would like to give one or two illustrations of the defects of the bill before questioning the minister about the relationship between the bill and the government's immigration record. The minister's first objective is to establish and obtain demographic goals with respect to the size, rate of growth, structure and geographic distribution of the Canadian population. What does this mean? The government does not tell us how it will establish its demographic goals. It does not even define the term "demographic". We can only guess at the intention of the
March 16, 1977

government. Does the government mean that it will decide how many people will live here and there, and what their origins must be? If this, or anything like it, is so, I want to know what right a democratic government has to determine the composition and nature of a nation. There is a reminiscence of George Orwell here, and I do not like it. I am sure most Canadians will be equally concerned. The minister should tell us what he really has in mind.
The bill also states that the government will enrich and strengthen the cultural and social fabric of Canada by taking into account the federal and bilingual nature of the nation. Here is another fuzzy area. What does the government really mean? Bilingualism certainly has a number of different meanings in Canada today. In Windsor it may mean the forceful introduction of French schools over the objections of local residents. In Quebec it means French only for immigrants. I do not think the minister should allow any doubt to exist in this matter. Some people may feel that the government intends to continue catering to Quebec by ignoring legislation like Bill 22 and by sending to that province immigrants who are Frenchspeaking or who are prepared to accept the racial policies of the Parti Quebecois and the previous Liberal administration. What does it mean for the rest of Canada? Are we to continue to receive large numbers of non English-speaking immigrants who are encouraged to retain their languages and customs? I think the minister should come clean and tell us what he really has in mind.
I would also like to know what the minister means when he states that we must not discriminate in the selection of immigrants on the grounds of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, or sex. This sounds more like a pious hope than an immigration policy. I am sure all Canadians wish to be fair and want their government to judge a man by his qualities rather than by his appearance or origin. However, having said that, I wonder whether Canadians would support an immigration policy which could make a fundamental change in the nature of Canada's population.
Surely the people who come to this country do so to join us, not to change us. So it must be advantageous for us to recruit people who are most likely to adapt to our way of life. Charity begins at home, and whatever we do in immigration should be geared to the interests of the Canadians who are now here, so in that sense, surely, it is important for us to discriminate. But once again the minister should make his position crystal clear. If he wants to turn Canada into a multiracial society without roots and without unity, then he should tell us. If he is really giving lip service to old cliches, then he should tell us that as well.
I am also troubled by the inference that the government may allow its immigration policy to be influenced by foreign governments. I suspect that this may have happened in the past, and I hope that my suspicions are unfounded. When the government states that one of its basic policies will be to meet its international legal obligations with respect to refugees and to uphold its humanitarian traditions with respect to the displaced and the persecuted, I wonder what this really means.
Immigration Act
If the minister intends to follow automatically the lead of the United Nations, then we may find ourselves supporting refugees of one type but not another. Events in Africa could easily lead us to a racial situation of the very worst type, and I do not think we should be tied to an international obligation that would place us in this position. Will the minister tell us precisely what the government has in mind?
While I am dealing with this subject I would like to have the minister's assurance that foreign governments are not involved in Canada's immigration program and that there has never been a foreign government involved in an immigration movement that has taken place without the knowledge or consent of this House. I am not talking about colonial times; I am referring to the more modern period that began after World War II. I am a little amused by the last objective, and if the government really means it, I must say it is long overdue. The problem, of course, is how the government is going to manage it. The bill states that Canada should promote international order and justice by denying the use of Canadian territory to persons who are likely to engage in criminal activity. All I can say to this is, "Thank God the government has finally come to its senses". But what is it going to do about the international criminals who are already here? The minister should tell us how many criminals are living in Canada illegally. He should list the number of persons with criminal records who have been permitted to remain in Canada in spite of such criminal records during the last five years, giving the reasons why these people were permitted to remain.
Now let me come back to my question. Does this government's past performance justify the kind of trust it is requesting? During the last ten years Canadian immigration policy has been a national disgrace. There seems to be no rhyme or reason to the way in which it is handled, and I often have the impression that it has been running along out of control and out of harmony with national interests. This may not be justified, but my concern is shared by many others, and now that we are discussing the whole question of immigration the minister has an opportunity to put the record straight.
The problem of illegal immigrants must be fully outlined and considered. As I understand it, these people came to Canada as visitors and then stayed without obtaining immigration status. Most of them were people who could not meet our overseas selection standards or were barred from entering Canada because they were criminals, subversives, or in other prohibited classes. As they were permitted to enter without any form of registration or screening, there was no way of determining whether they were still in Canada after their visits were over.
How did we get into this mess? The costs have been staggering and the government has ended up allowing tens of thousands of workers to remain here who do not have anything like the minimum qualifications that are normally required, while others are lined up at immigration offices around the world. This has created imbalances in our labour force, taken jobs away from Canadian workers, placed great strains on our social welfare services, and is an important reason for our

March 16, 1977
Immigration Act
current unemployment situation. I want to know what has happened and who was responsible for it. When our party was in office, immigration was under the management of the Hon. Ellen Fairclough, and later under the Hon. Richard A. Bell. Most visitors, other than persons from a few countries like the United States, the United Kingdom and France, required visitors' visas to enter Canada. This gave us their names, and if they overstayed we knew who we were looking for. But even more important, the requirements screened out most criminals and subversives because they did not present themselves to our overseas officers.
When was this system changed? Who changed it? Why was it changed? Did the people responsible for the change understand where their actions would lead? The minister should list the names of all people who participated in these deliberations, with details about their advice and why it was or was not taken. He should also indicate how the situation will be handled under the new legislation.
One of our great economic problems is the low productivity of our labour force. There is no doubt that illegal immigrants who do not meet our worker requirements have contributed to this problem, but I understand that the entire flow of immigrant workers, when balanced against Canadians who migrate to other countries, does not give us the occupational balance that is needed to improve or maintain our productivity. Some time ago the immigration branch worked out a scheme with most of the provinces for surveys to determine the provincial worker requirements that should be filled through immigration. I am told by provincial officials that when the immigration flow was geared to this program it was very successful, but it was suddenly stopped without explanation. Would the minister tell us how long the program ran, who was responsible for it, and, most important, why it was stopped? He should also indicate how the new legislation will work in this area and what provision, if any, is being made for the systematic involvement of the provinces.
Some of my colleagues believe that most of the current immigration problems began back in 1966 and 1967, just after the old department of citizenship and immigration became the Department of Manpower and Immigration. They still talk about the extraordinary events that took place during the discussions on the 1966 white paper on immigration. As most of us were not here at that time it would be helpful if the minister would tell us what really happened. I have read the white paper. It is an interesting document. The words were right. But why were the results so different? Perhaps it will be clearer if I quote from the paper, which states:
-tbc unproductive worker, exposed to unemployment, will be the uneducated one who lacks the capacity for learning new, more complex skills... the productivity of the work force should not be offset by the immigration policy as it would be if a large proportion of the immigrants were unskilled.
This sounds great, and it is certainly an approach that could be supported by members on all sides of the House who have the best interests of the nation at heart. My colleagues who were here at that time tell me they went to the initial meetings
(Mr. Ritchie.]
of the parliamentary committee, convened to consider the white paper's proposals, with great expectations. But to their surprise it became clear that Liberal backbenchers on the committee were against their own government's position and began a campaign to have it changed. Meetings were held all through the winter of 1966-67 and they gradually became less and less productive. One by one the good ideas were discarded. Departmental officials had little to contribute and began to act as technical advisers. One provincial official from my province sat up half the night preparing for the questions he expected after the presentation of his brief. He was amazed whep he was not asked one significant question. Then, suddenly, the whole process ended.
On April 11, 1967, Jean Marchand, now Senator Mar-chand, told the committee that the white paper would be abandoned and he unveiled a completely new plan. Our members had spent the whole winter discussing a formal government proposal which was abandoned in 20 minutes without an opportunity for discussion. They thought they would be asked to consider a new plan, but there were no more meetings. It was a highly unusual move. Now that we are considering a new Immigration Act, I think the minister should tell us what happened.
When Mr. Marchand said that the white paper would be set aside he indicated that his department had devised a point-rating scheme for the selection of immigrant workers, and then he increased the number of classes that could be nominated by distant relatives. Rather curiously, in spite of what he had stated in the white paper, he stressed the importance of personal suitability over education and occupational training. He said that a brother would not be admissible solely because he was a brother, but he would be admissible as long as he ranked very modestly in the other selection categories. Provided he had good personal qualities, he would be admissible virtually without skill or education.
What did he mean? I think the minister should explain it in detail. Did he really mean that workers would be allowed to enter Canada without skills and educational levels needed in the labour force? I have noted that the percentage of unskilled immigrants entering Canada that year was 32 per cent higher than it was the previous year. Why was this allowed to happen at a time when the percentage of unskilled persons in the labour force had been steadily dropping at the rate of about 27 per cent for five or six years? At the same time unemployment was rising, as it is today, and the same Mr. Marchand had previously said that the unproductive worker would be the uneducated one who lacked the capacity for learning new or complex skills.
Mr. Marchand abandoned the white paper in April. Four months later an order in council was passed to introduce the new point-rating system. Why did it take so long? It would be helpful if the minister would tell us what really happened during this period. When was the rating system really established? Who were the people responsible for it? Did it require changes or modifications after its initial introduction? If so,
March 16, 1977

what were the reasons for the changes, and who authorized them?
Now I want to turn to a very serious matter that requires immediate clarification. For some time it has been rumoured that the immigration department had used unofficial quotas to control immigration from our traditional sources of immigration. I should tell the minister that I find this extremely difficult to accept, but I want his assurance that it has never happened, and will never happen in the future.
I have also heard that immigration advertising in some of the traditional countries was substantially reduced and that this was done at a time when offices were being opened in other countries where it was obvious that we could only obtain large percentages of unskilled applicants. I would like the minister to comment on this as well and tell us if there has ever been an instance where this has occurred. It would be a sorry day for Canada if it should turn out that this government has restricted the flow of traditional immigrant workers while encouraging the flow of unskilled people.
I have heard reports that one deputy minister of immigration told a representative of the provincial government that he would limit the flow of immigrants from one traditional country regardless of that province's requirements for skilled and professional workers, and that no explanation was given. It was even suggested that some kind of mathematical formula would be applied to restrict immigration flows from certain areas. I find this incredible and I want the minister's assurances that it has never happened.
I understand that one of the planks of the proposed legislation is the idea that people who are willing to go to designated areas where their services are in greater demand will be given preferential consideration at the time of selection. The idea sounds great-but does the minister really think it will work? I understand that it is not a new idea and it was tried out in the early 1950s and abandoned. I wonder if the minister will tell us about the the early farm workers, about the track workers' programs? I would like him to explain why they were not successful and describe some of the by-products of fraud and manipulation that went with them. There is no point starting back into the same old problem area. I want the minister to describe his reasoning.
In conclusion, let me say that I am not satisfied with the provisions of this bill. If it becomes law, the department will be able to go on its own course without parliamentary approval or understanding. Its track record, even in the few illustrations I have given, certainly does not justify this kind of power. On the other hand, if the minister will sit down with us openly and will honestly confide in us in the committee, we may be able to come to a mutually satisfactory position that will be in the interest of all Canadians.

My grandparents came to this country from southern Russia 102 years ago. They left Russia because the political climate of the country was volatile then, as it was for several generations afterwards, and because they were concerned about the future of their family. They did not want to raise their family in that political climate. They were people of very strong religious beliefs. They wanted to pass those beliefs, values and traditions on to their children, and knew that if they stayed in Russia those opportunities would be jeopardized and family life would not remain as it had been. So they left, at considerable economic disadvantage, and moved to the prairies of our country. They lived in sod-houses. They lived in southern Manitoba and moved to Saskatchewan before Saskatchewan was a province and was part of the Northwest Territories.
Later, my parents lived in an isolated part of British Columbia. Being concerned about the conditions under which their family was growing up, they decided to move again, once more at considerable economic disadvantage, from that isolated area of British Columbia to a more populated area of Canada in order to give their family the benefit of all the advantages which could accrue to them. Again it was the family that was most important to them. One thing that I have appreciated about my grandparents and parents-and I know that other members can say the same-is that they passed those values on to me. In my home the family is the most important thing to me. The minister has sat there and nodded his head, saying in effect that he will provide the regulations at committee stage. All he will do is nod his head. He will never put it on the record.
I wish the minister would say emphatically and unequivocally that the regulations will be before the committee for open discussion, the committee will be responsible for the revision of those regulations, and that they will be the regulations under which the immigration department will operate. Right now we do not know what we are debating because the operative part of the act is in the regulations. Let me illustrate. I turn to page 2 of the bill, the definition stage. Under the word "family" I read:
"family", for the purpose of any provision of this act, has such meaning as is prescribed for the purpose of that provision-

That was obviously written by a bureaucrat. What in the world does it mean? Where are we going with that kind of definition? Who knows what it means? I turn to page 60 of the bill. Under "Regulations" It reads:
115. (1) The governor in council may make regulations (c) exempting members of the family class from any of the requirements of the regulations and prescribing, in substitution for such regulations, special regulations for the purpose of determining the ability and willingness of persons who sponsor applications for landing to assist such members in becoming successfully established in Canada,
Nowhere in the bill do we have a clear definition or statement as to what is a family. Every culture is entitled to its definition of a family. However, we do not know what that definition is. How else would the minister and his department work on immigration, not ceilings but targets, as he calls it? I was a member of that committee and I recall the many hours we spent struggling with the formulation of recommendations. I also remember hearing people all across Canada saying, "I guess this is another government exercise which will cost close to a million dollars, but what is likely to come out of it? Again I challenge the minister. The committee
March 16, 1977

Mr. Speaker, I have here a copy of the flow chart of the implementation network which the minister and his officials have outlined. speechtext:
Has he something to hide? Do the Canadian people not have a right to know what the implications will be? If he has nothing to hide, he will share them with us. Another of the views expressed by the special parliamentary committee studying the green paper read as follows:
The committee objects to the practice of issuing regulations under the guise of confidential departmental directives.
Again I would remind the hon. gentleman that all across Canada citizens were coming to us saying, "Is there to be any kind of comparison possible between the findings of the committee and the new immigration bill?" The most significant thing which in my view identified the bill before us with the old act is the fact that in both cases the regulations are being kept from the Canadian public. All we can do is read the Canada Gazette to see whether the regulations have been changed, and then we can find out what departmental policy is at a particular time. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is pretty shabby treatment of the Canadian people. I should like to illustrate what I mean.
Just a few days ago I received from the department the quarterly statistics manual, "Migration, '76" showing migration statistics up to the third quarter of 1976. As everyone knows, we are facing an unemployment crisis in our country; one million people are unemployed. So I was naturally interested in seeing what the Department of Immigration was doing in relation to the number of immigrants coming to this country in a time of such high unemployment.
On page 8, in table 3, the department outlines the flow of immigrants by occupational groups and province of destination. I may say I find this to be a very helpful document and I am grateful to the minister and to the department for sending it to us. But I was amazed to find out some of the things that are happening. Under the heading "Teaching" I find that in the first three quarters of 1976, 1,998 teachers came to Canada-effectively, 2,000 in the first nine months of the year. I do not have my finger on the need for teachers all across this country, but I do know that in British Columbia teachers are looking for jobs and I am sure that is true of other provinces as well. Yet I find that the department of immigration brought in, as I say, 2,000 teachers in the first nine months of 1976. I see here that Quebec, with 10 per cent unemployment, received 409 of these teachers, and Ontario 711. I wonder whether the Teachers' Federation of Ontario is aware of the number of teachers who came to Canada last
Immigration Act
year, and particularly to that province, in face of the unemployment picture today. The number of new teachers admitted to British Columbia was 263.
What startles me is that in order to qualify to come to Canada these teachers have supposedly to apply to the professional division of Canada Manpower in the central offices of large provinces; they have to qualify in the professional centres before coming here to work. I do not know about the experience of other hon. members, but any time I have gone to the Manpower office in my riding I have found they are very honest with me. They say, "Unemployment is running at about 9>/4 per cent and we cannot really do very much." Any time I try to intervene on behalf of a constituent to help bring someone into the country under the unification of families policy, a Manpower official says, "Yes, but with the unemployment figures we are facing today it really cannot be done." So I run up against a brick wall.
Nevertheless, we find that in a nine-month period 263 teachers came to British Columbia. Let me go down the list. Clerical workers. I would imagine that with unemployment running at 7V4 per cent across Canada, 10 per cent in Quebec, between 15 per cent and 20 per cent in the Maritimes, and about 8 per cent in British Columbia, clerical people are looking for jobs everywhere. There should be people lining up for clerical positions. Yet I find that in nine months no fewer than 7,478 clerical people were brought into Canada. Of those, 1,303 went to Quebec, 3,864 went to Ontario, and 1,101 went to British Columbia. Just a few weeks ago I tried to find a job for a secretary in British Columbia. I called up the Manpower office and asked whether there was any shortage of secretaries in the province. I was told that these people were Coming out of his ears, that he had more than he could handle. Yet the immigration department ratifies admission of 7,500 in nine months-all by regulation!
As for sales, I guess this is another area in which jobs ought easily to be filled. In a period of high unemployment many people who are unemployed would gladly take on a sales position if only they could get a job. The immigration department brought into Canada 2,040 sales persons in nine months, and I am wondering what the hundreds, if not thousands, of unemployed sales people would think if they found out that some 2,000 extra sales people were admitted to this country by the immigration minister. Of that number, 414 went to Quebec, 999 to Ontario and 332 to British Columbia.
In the area of machinists we are facing a critical situation, yet 2,400 came to Canada in nine months, from where I do not know. I wonder whether the machinists union is aware of that? With 10 per cent unemployment in Quebec, 400 machinists went to the province, and 158 went to British Columbia. In the fabricating trade, 6,533 people were admitted to Canada. Of that number, 1,769 went to Quebec. Just think of all the textile workers who are unemployed in that province, yet the immigration department brought into the province another
