1,700. In addition, 2,782 went to the province of Ontario, and 671 toB.C.
As for the construction trades, we are facing a decline in the construction industry and a lot of construction workers are out of work, as well as carpenters, carpenters' helpers, masons- you name it, Mr. Speaker. Despite this, the immigration department brought into Canada 3,208 construction workers. With one million unemployed in this country, do we want to bring in additional construction workers? Of that 3,208, 388 went to the province of Quebec, 1,573 went to Ontario and 399 went to British Columbia. I know that in the lower mainland of British Columbia there are construction workers who would like to have a job.
Is the department serious about enforcing its regulations governing the need for a manpower permit to enter Canada? How is it that 400 construction workers in nine months enter British Columbia, in view of the kind of unemployment that industry is facing there? The number admitted in nine months was 48,590, but with their dependants, amounting to 68,921, the total figure in the first nine months of last year for immigration was 117,511.
I am not concerned so much with the total number of immigrants; rather, I go back to the time when I represented people who were dealing with immigration officers and manpower officers in an effort to help them unify their families in Canada. Or there have been occasions when a businessman has come to me and told me he needs a man who is qualified to do a certain kind of work. I would tell him to go the Manpower and to have Manpower advertise the job for 30 days all across Canada. If in 30 days no one applies for the job, then I tell him he can bring in a person from outside. I think that is a fair arrangement if everyone were playing by the same rules. However, I have struck out every time except once. Only once was I successful in helping an employer bring an employee into Canada, and that was because no one else in Canada could do the job, which was a very esoteric and unusual one. On every other occasion Manpower has advertised jobs across Canada.
When I see these immigration figures, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what is going on, whether there is one regulation for one group of people and another regulation for another group. If, for example, there is an oversupply of staff in jobs such as sales, how is it that by the department's own admission 2,040 sales persons were brought into Canada? I have no objection to people coming to this country, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is wholesome for Canada to have an infusion of immigrants. But the same rules should apply to everyone, and somehow I do not think this is the case.
This reminds me of a man who came to me several months ago. He had lived for some years in one of the British possessions in the Third World and had raised his family there. Finally he decided to move to Canada. His adult son decided to move back to England, where he worked in a professional capacity chartering cargo planes. This young man is the only member of that family in England; I do not think he has even an uncle or a cousin there. All the members of the family live

in different parts of the world, but his parent and one sibling are in Canada.
Having read press reports concerning the government's policy on family reunification, the father went to the local immigration office and applied for his son to come to Canada. In effect, the immigration officer said he would try, but that since he was now an adult he had to apply under the independent category. He applied, and naturally was struck out. Finally, the father called me and I contacted not only the local official, who was as helpful as he could be under the regulations, but also the immigration officer in London to see whether he could find some ingredient which would enable the one son left in England to come to Canada. But, Mr. Speaker, there was no way.
The government says it believes in the reunification of families, but I go back to what the hon. member for Vancouver East said. The government wants to parade itself to the Canadian people as believing in the reunification of families, but when I try to reunify one family it does not work out that way. This policy is good only for certain people. I have yet to be successful in bringing that young man over to Canada, even though he is the only member of that family left in England. Is that justice? Something has to be done, and that is what I mean about the injustice of having the regulations separate from the bill. The minister seems determined to make sure that we will never see them and debate them on the floor of the House, and the Canadian people will be kept in the dark as to how the immigration policy of our country will operate. And they call this the just society!
There are a couple of other aspects of the bill which give me cause for concern. I think the whole area of the refugee class is something we should reconsider. I reiterate that we are members of the Canadian family or are members indirectly because we left a country or our forefathers left a country for political reasons. I have a great deal of sympathy for those people, and more than sympathy, compassion, for those who are faced with a future in a country that is hostile to their convictions and where their life is at stake. But in the intervening years, in the last 100 years, we have been facing a new philosophy in this world; that is, the philosophy of pragmatism which says that whatever works is right, that there is no such thing as absolute morality. Truth is truth if it works, and it is no longer truth it it does not work. That is pragmatism.
There are a lot of political activists across the world who believe in that philosophy and who are politically active in their country. They even believe in the violent overthrow of their country. Their morality is based on pragmatism. What we have to define for ourselves is what their relationship would be to our way of life here. We would be totally irresponsible Canadians, and certainly irresponsible legislators, if we did not examine thoroughly the implications of that philosophy as it pertains to the immigration policy.
Surely we owe it to ourselves, to the future of our country, to our children and to our children's children, to make sure

March 16, 1977

that the people who want to come to Canada are those who believe in the validity of our institutions, who want to see our way of life perpetuated and who believe in democracy as we know it today. But more and more we see around the world societies and political systems that do not hold to our way of life. It is all too easy to declare yourself a refugee from that kind of society. I reiterate that we need to be very understanding of the plight of refugees, but it seems to me that the United Nations' declaration may be a little too tolerant in that area. Certainly, I do not think we should allow them to define, in Canada, whether or not they are political refugees.
If I understand the act correctly, one of its provisions is that the judge who is adjudicating the final stages of a refugee's disposition within Canada must ask of that refugee, "Are you a political refugee"? If you do not believe in the absolute right or wrong, or the absolute truth, and you are pragmatist, then surely anything you say can be justified; and if the judge asks you whether you are a political refugee, then of course you are going to say "Yes" if it means staying within the country rather than being deported to your hostile homeland. Somehow we will have to come to grips with this provision in the Immigration Act. I reiterate that we need to be very compassionate and understanding of the plight of the refugees, but we have to do it in the knowledge of the new philosophy which exists in our society.
Finally, there is one other provision in the bill which I believe should be examined carefully. I think this provision was drafted with the intent of being more fair and finding a more operative and equitable way of admitting people into Canada. It has to do with what is called the inadmissible classes. What concerns me about this is the fact that there are about 750,000 people who apply to come to Canada every year, and there are probably 1.5 million who want to come, but only half of them take the first step, that is, to apply to come to Canada. Even under the present regulations most of them are refused. There are six or seven times as many people who apply to come to Canada as are admitted to this country.
With that kind of reservoir of people of whom probably 99.9999 per cent would be wholesome contributors to our way of life, it concerns me that we want to spend so much time examining the ways in which we can get people to come to the country who might be a threat to our society. Why should we spend so much time on that when there are so many people who would appreciate the opportunity of living here and who would contribute to the welfare of our society? I think all members would agree that for some classes of people it has been too difficult in times past to come in, and I am glad to see provisions in the bill which eliminate the discriminatory aspects of the bill, such as health provisions and so forth. But in the previous act they were the so-called prohibited class. Now the drafters have used some cosmetics; they have used a less offensive term and they are calling this group of people the "inadmissible class."
As I look at the provision, I see it as a nightmare for the people who are supposed to administer the act to find ways of making it as equitable as they want it to be. Is it the intent of
Immigration Act
the act to make sure that people who have been convicted of crime in their country are treated the same way under our system of jurisprudence?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will conclude my remarks in a couple of minutes. I cannot help but think that under this provision we are creating more problems than we can solve. If we are to take our Criminal Code and superimpose it over the criminal codes of every other country in the world, what a nightmare that will be. We would have an army of bureaucrats trying to make sure that every provision of the Criminal Code matched a similar provision in other criminal codes. Can you imagine what kind of a job that would be? In the United Nations alone there are 150 countries, each with its own lifestyle, traditions and set of values. What is a crime in Canada is not necessarily a crime in other countries. How in the world will we standardize our laws? I think we have good intentions, but how are we going to do that? These are the things the minister and his officials have not examined thoroughly enough. They have to be examined further if we are going to have a bill which will benefit Canadians now and in the future.
I will conclude by saying, as I said at the outset, that the immigration bill has probably the most far-reaching implications for Canada of any bill we will be debating in this session and probably in this parliament. It behooves us, as legislators, to examine this bill more carefully and to demand of the minister good stewardship of his department. The minister should provide the regulations so that we can examine them and be responsible for them, as we ought to be. If he will do that, he will be doing a service both to parliament and to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the House that my speech will be short. This has been a lengthy debate and I do not want to jar its tenor in any way. I simply want to contribute two points to the debate before it is wound up by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald).
The first point I would like to make is with reference to refugees. We need a better procedure for refugees, and I hope this bill will provide a procedure to take care of cases like the one about which I am going to talk. This case concerns a teenager whose uncle moved to Canada and established a very successful business in Halifax-East Hants. When trouble broke out in Lebanon, the young man managed to move to Cyprus. He was in a position to move to Canada at a moment's notice if we had had a procedure for making him a Canadian citizen. His uncle here wished to adopt him. His parents wished that he could have that right. They were prepared to give their son

Immigration Act
up, and under all the circumstances it seemed to me to add up to a pretty humanitarian type of situation. However, there was great frustration in trying to bring it about. There was frustration in dealing with the regulations in the act which we have now. There was frustration in dealing with the school system in Nova Scotia and in dealing with a dozen and one things, including the attitude of the bureaucracy in Cyprus. So, all in all, what seemed to me to have been a step which should have been taken very quickly turned out to be a step which even with the best help of those in the minister's office here in Ottawa we were not able to take.
I am prepared to share my frustration with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) in the committee and to present this as a classic case in which there should have been not only more discretion but also the ability to move rather quickly. This matter has really bothered me and I present it for the public record now. However, when the committee is asked to deal with the refugee part of this bill I would like to have at least five minutes in the sun.
There is another point about which the House might expect me to speak at more length than I will, and that is the point about regulations. Regulations sometimes take on horrendous or even Frankensteinian-monster proportions to the people in this place and in the other place. For reasons which are probably pretty apparent, having worked in the committee which deals with regulations I know that one can live with a certain type of regulation, but with other regulations it is very difficult indeed. Those who argue that the regulations should be seen beforehand make a very good argument. I think the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, whose attention I hope to get eventually, would be well advised to take the same attitude as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) about the proposed regulations under the gun law; that is to say, they shall be looked at in committee before the act becomes final. I think that was a very useful precedent in our parliamentary process. We all know that that particular bill did not go to its final conclusion, but the fact that that offer was made was, to my mind, a substantial improvement over anything we have seen before with regard to regulations. I hope the Minister of Manpower and Immigration will accept this proposal as being reasonable.
I do not think it hurts to have proposed regulations examined from the standpoint of the criteria which have been adopted both in this House and in the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. I gather I am not to have the ear of the minister, but perhaps my contribution can be drawn to his attention. I make my proposal very seriously. Perhaps I can repeat that it would be a very useful step, when new legislation which contains broad powers for dealing with problems by way of regulation is introduced, to have the regulations attached to it brought in so that they can be examined. They do not necessarily need to be examined in the committee which I have the honour to head; I think they should be examined in the committee which deals with the legislation.
[Mr. McCleave.)
In that committee there are likely to be experts. For example, I am looking at my friend, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), and I think many things should be brought into the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry by way of regulation so that he can have the first crack at them, rather than the Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments. As we all know, the legislation dealing with statutory instruments provides that future regulations shall be presented to that committee.
The second thing is that some of the tactics the privy council office has used on our parliamentary committee to keep future regulations away from that committee should be restricted. I said I would speak only for a brief period of time, but I make these points sincerely. I would be inclined to raise hell, if I may use that word, if no regard was paid to the two small representations I have made this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read with interest some of the remarks made earlier in the debate. I did not have the opportunity to hear them all firsthand. However, I listened carefully to some remarks today. The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) said that this bill is likely the most important legislation we will deal with in this parliament, and I know other people have made similar statements. I believe that the whole subject of immigration and migration policy as it affects the jurisdiction of the federal government is indeed a major responsibility. I do not think anyone, no matter what his views with respect to this important and, at times, controversial subject, would say otherwise.
There are a couple of basic questions which I think have to be examined at the outset with respect to the legislation which is before us. I suppose the principal question which must be asked at some point in the process is why new immigration legislation is being proposed. Perhaps that is an overly obvious question to ask, since it has been well documented by the minister and others who have participated in this debate that a process has gone on for three or four years which has involved the initial commitment of his predecessor, the publication of the green paper and supporting documents, the reference to the special committee, the work of that special committee, its report, obviously made after lengthy consideration on the part of the committee and, finally, this legislation.
I think this question must be raised at the outset: Why are we launched on this particular process? The best argument I have been able to hear, either from the minister, his officials or his predecessor, is that the legislation of 1952 is obviously obsolete. It is obvious that the reference to obsolescence has as its basis those prohibited classes which now are an anachronism. They bring to mind words like moral turpitude, epilepsy, and the names of other illnesses which in all justice we would not want to see included today in any legal definition.
If the intent was primarily to remove the obsolescence built into the present legislation, one feels that it would not have been necessary to embark on such a major process involving special reports, special committees, examinations by special
March 16, 1977

committees, concluded by a fairly lengthy debate on this matter in parliament. Obviously, much more is at stake than the occasional anachronism in a piece of legislation.
There have been, as I suppose the minister and his officials may say, very real pressures for a new act which could give us some kind of new approach, a more modern approach, to the question of immigration. I think we come closer to the truth when we hear the minister or his officials talking about more effective management of the immigration program. We use certain code words, Mr. Speaker, and when certain public people use code words in talking about immigration we must examine those words most carefully. I am of the firm belief that some of the code words have to do with management, efficiency, the effectiveness of resources and some of the other things listed in the objectives set out in this bill for the first time, to which I shall refer in a moment. Those code words should be looked at carefully and as penetratingly as possible, because they may tell us a good deal about the real intentions of the government, the minister and his officials.
I believe that the government is attempting to respond, perhaps even reinforce, some perceptions which have received a good deal of publicity and discussion during the past few years. Those perceptions do not see immigration as a kind of objective or neutral social phenomenon; they see it as being a major problem, a major social difficulty which we must confront and somehow solve.
It seems strange to me that almost everybody seems to believe we are dealing with a difficult and complex problem, a problem which somehow must be controlled, managed and brought under effective jurisdiction. I find this a disturbing concept from two points of view. It disturbs me because it flies in the face of the evolution of this country. Numerous speakers on both sides of the House have indicated, as they have shown with documented evidence, that we are in a very real sense a nation of immigrants. I think the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) mentioned that something like ten million immigrants have come here since confederation. Clearly, at present more than half the population consists of either first, second or third generation Canadians or is related to those who originally came here as immigrants within the last 100 years. Indeed, some time ago, when reflecting on the public attitudes of a couple of years ago and of a decade ago when Mr. Marchand introduced the white paper and amendments to the Immigration Act, I looked at a number of editorials which were written a decade ago. I examined a good deal of the publicity which had surrounded the introduction of that white paper.
I have the white paper here, but I will not quote from it. If hon. members read it, it should become obviously and painfully apparent to them that this same government, under a different leader and minister but listening to essentially the same bureaucratic advisers, took the position about a decade ago that immigration was a powerful tool, a powerful process which has been extremely valuable in the total development of this country. One recalls the rhetoric surrounding various events of our nation's history, the appeals by public figures to
Immigration Act
Europeans and statements about this great land of promise, Canada. We know the extent to which previous governments in our history invested large sums of money in order to ensure an adequate flow of new Canadians to populate this country and open its virgin territories. As late as a decade ago, indeed, after we had existed for more than 100 years as a nation, this government was able to talk in positive terms about the continuing phenomenon of immigration as being an asset to the further development-the exploitation, if you like-and exploration of this country.
The green paper produced two or three years ago contained none of that positive, buoyant atmosphere. It was, indeed, a document which left one with the feeling that although immigration perhaps was not an evil it was a problem, and that if we did not cope with it we would find ourselves living in a social situation which could rapidly get out of control. When we are told we need a new immigration act, it is not just a question of revising or eliminating anachronisms in a piece of legislation 25 years old; it may, indeed, be turning around the question of immigration. That is what has bothered me so seriously about the measures which the minister has brought before the House in this bill.
We are not debating a piece of legislation which would enshrine Canada's continued belief in the importance of having new people come here with new ideas to populate this country, although there is lip service paid in the objectives to those kinds of values and cultural advantages-but they are far down the list when compared with advantages of trade and commerce. Lip service is paid to the notion of effectively regulating, managing, controlling and dispersing the immigration phenomenon of this country.
We have been taken in, Mr. Speaker. When problems have developed concerning unemployment, inadequate or unavailable housing in urban centres and the occasional reports of racial or ethnic disturbances or confrontations, we have allowed extremists in our society to propagate the belief that immigration is a problem and that we must effectively control this dangerous gene of immigration. I suggest that the seeds of such beliefs were sowed ten years ago with the introduction of the points system, because that system allowed us to enunciate a new kind of discrimination.
At root, what bothers many people about the green paper is that it considers immigration as a problem. Basically, it sees immigration as negative, as something to be managed. It is much more concerned about systems management than about dealing with people as people. That, certainly, is the atmosphere pervading this legislation. The points system, to which I will refer in a moment, laid the groundwork of a new kind of discrimination with which we have had some years of experience. I say, at the outset, that in a sense we have turned the subject of immigration on its head. I think we should all be clear about what has happened to us, because all of us have to some degree fallen into an enormous trap. The trap is simple, but many threads and nuances run through it. It is that immigration is no longer to be considered as basically a

March 16, 1977
Immigration Act
positive force; it is no longer to be considered as essential to the further unfolding of this country.
This is, in fact, increasingly a problem-oriented situation which must be increasingly controlled, regulated and brought under some kind of effective systems management. It has also been a very convenient scapegoat, particularly for government apologists or others who want to blame many of the social ills of our country on those who are new or different. We should not be surprised at this. This is not something altogether different from other societies.
If we study some of the social development and cultures to the south of us, or in Great Britain, and the problems that have arisen with regard to urban slums, unemployment and abrasiveness of situations which exist in educational centres, all have caused people to look for some effective solution or basic cause as to why we are faced with these particular problems. If we can point to the stranger, the person with a different accent, different customs, different language or different skin colour and blame many of the problems of our society on those we regard, quite frankly, as outsiders and strangers, that is a very dangerous situation for any society to arrive at. To be aware of that in the context of this debate is certainly to be very irresponsible. To allow for the growth of these kinds of myths is to strengthen beliefs and harden situations which will make it more difficult in the final analysis to solve some of the very real social and economic problems that we face.
The objectives set out in the bill claim that this will allow, for the first time, as the minister said in his press release at the time of the tabling of the bill:
The bill explicitly affirms, for the first time, the fundamental objectives of Canadian immigration law; family reunification, non-discrimination, concern for refugees, and the promotion of Canada's economic, social, demographic and cultural goals.
It is noteworthy that in spite of the government being preoccupied with this matter for the better part of three or four years, neither this minister nor his predecessor have given us a very firm indication as to our economic, social, demographic and cultural goals. The furthest we seem to get on this is some statement by the minister that there will be a process of consultation before such things as levels or quotas are arrived at. Clause 3(f) of the bill reads:
-to ensure that any person who seeks admission to Canada on either a permanent or temporary basis is subject to standards of admission that do not discriminate on grounds of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion or sex-
To use the word "non-discrimination" to apply to that is certainly something I would hope all, or almost all of the people in Canada would strongly support. It is in line with previous declarations that have been made in the past ten-year period. Certainly, it was an important step forward in making that kind of assertion. I say that because, as I think previous speakers have mentioned, our record with respect to complete neutrality and non-discrimination concerning Oriental and Asian immigrants is not one of which any of us can be proud. The situation with regard to the Chinese, Japanese and Indian people has been one that should give us all cause for thought,
when we are all inclined to say all too quickly that Canada has had a great and long tradition of non-discrimination when it comes to race.
What disturbs me is that while the minister has enshrined in the objectives admirable sentiments, which I think are agreed to by many other countries similar to Canada, the points system as it has been established and as it will apparently continue will indeed perpetuate if not exacerbate discimination in other areas with which we have yet to come to grips.
It may be true that we do not discriminate against those who are of different racial origin, but very clearly our points system discriminates against the poor. It may be true that we do not discriminate against those who have another creed, but we very clearly discriminate against those of lesser education or sophistication. It may be true that we do not have any particular discrimination against people from any particular origin, but it is true that we locate our offices and the processing of those who apply for immigration very much with a view to origin and geographic location. As I have said, the points system discriminates very much in favour of those who are already here. It is a self-serving one, self-serving in a negative sense in that those of us who are here feel increasingly threatened by those who want to come.
There is, within the context of this kind of points system, a sort of siege mentality which, given the kind of world we live in, will increase interaction between nationalities, groups and cultures which is exceedingly dangerous. In fact, the points system is a kind of clever put-down of those of different economies, societies and cultures. Behind much of the debate on points and quotas is the very real question of a protection of privileges. There is in a sense an attempt to achieve a kind of monolithic, cultural and economic enclave. While an enclave may have some appeal on a short-term basis, its long-term virtues for all the citizens of this county are greatly to be doubted.
It is important that we realize the sense of the Immigration Act is to move, not toward a more open society but toward a more closed one, one that will require more regulations and more rules and regulations that are not really public knowledge. I shall mention that again, because I think the lack of commitment on the part of this minister to, in effect, explain how the act is going to operate is nothing short of shocking, given the importance of this bill to every Canadian.
I would hope that within the time the bill is being debated on second reading, perhaps before we come back to debate it again, the minister will reflect on the numerous calls he has had from many members of this chamber for full disclosure of the regulations before we conclude second reading. Only in that way can we be sure that when the minister said future immigration levels are made a matter for open decision and public announcement in advance by the government, his commitment to such open decision will in fact be a credible one.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
